stories.content:
# Uncle Alan Palm Island's Story

That's a pretty good seed actually. Yeah. I reckon that's... Let's hope we don't run out of battery. What do you mean no battery? Are we shooting? Yeah, we're shooting. We talking? We could start. My first question. So we've been hanging out for a little bit. What's the best way for me to...
I'll just do... What do I call you? Call me Uncle Alan. Uncle? Uncle Alan? Yeah, and then I'll just do welcoming in. Do welcoming in and then we can roll. Okay. Yeah, you can talk to me. You don't have to talk to the camera. All right. Good morning, everyone. My name is Alan Palm Island. We are here on...
Bungaman Barra, Great Palm Island, Daru Maru. We look around Great Palm, all the rest of the islands around us, surrounding islands. And we are here today, a little bit myself. Our skin name is Nakawaraka, skin name. And our language name, our language is Mulkaal.
And we speak in our town that we speak our language, that we call it Nakarawaraka Purpanbara. You're welcome to Great Palm. But I say the Pukumanbara. Pukumanbara means Great Palm Island, Mambara. And Darumaru means the rest of the islands or surrounding islands.
Or Palm, Great Palm. And today, I just wanted to say that the islands behind me, it's Ngaru, they call it Kirisho. Ngaru up there, North Palm, and Guggenbaden. And across here, we've got Guggenbaden is Hoffia's Island.
And you got to cross over here to Amelia, which is Phantom Island. Great Palm is sitting on, as we got here on our emblem, is Mingna Mingna Ranges. And in this emblem, we have a...
Which we call a shield. We call Bukal. Bukal means shield. And we, we put, I put the designs on it as a tool because our boundary is, is come into form of a, of a big manta ray. Our boundary, we call it Mingana Mingana Ranges. Mingana Mingana. Our boundaries is that area of Great Palm Island. And in that area, we keep,
And I'm just trying to welcome you all today. Thanks for coming. And you go ahead. Super powerful. Pleasure to be here with you. Yeah, we can go lots of ways with this, but I think the first thing is how would you like to talk about yourself as a person from here? And how would you like to introduce...
Well, for myself, I got my totem. It's Kurenja. Kurenja means stingray. And that's where I got my totem because you can't eat my totem or you get sick. I said, no, I'll leave it as it is. Well, my highest...
I've been traveling a lot around myself. As a small boy, my father taught me how to paint. And as I was starting off, he just showed me how to use a charcoal and did a drawing on a piece of paper. And then I started...
Painting and I also learned from him also what he does. A lot of work of making buccal, making shields and making drums, island dance from when I was small and I just used to watch dad always paint and I just got to learn a lot about it and very interesting for me and me and my brother Reg, my elder brother. Reg and Walter, my elder brother. And whenever they go, I follow behind.
And they'd say, no, you can't come. You've got to go back. Get back. Yeah, well, they said, all right. And they'd come back. But I always go, and I learn things from my dad. But sometimes we grow, too. And eventually, we went on a different route now and started growing up.
We went to schools, and Dad always been busy, so we had to learn English and maths and that. Sometimes Dad always send us to do some paintings with some elders, people. But we learned what Dad taught me too, how to paint too, and painting the shields and all that too.
And for myself. Been travelling a lot when I left there from Palm and as I went to school, high schools and I did some, spread my wing out and go and travel around, looking around and checking out universities and TAFEs with arts, art colleges and all that.
I learned a lot from that. And from that, then I sort of think that I would rather come back home now and start doing better work for Mambara now. And today now, we started our Mingna Mingna rangers up and develop. And this is how we today now.
Thanks for that for all of us. We got the Bulkerman people also with us too. And they will work with us. Thank you. Amazing. I need to say this. I got to put in a platform. But is it still running? Yeah. We cut it. Yeah. I'd love to hear a little bit about what it was like being...
Being young and did you have a concept of what like this place was or culture was when you were young or were you just learning? What was that experience like? Well, my experience was, like I said, to go back when I was young and that was my, that was sort of planted on me, my dad and then I grew with it, see, but...
That's where I grew older and we had to go to learn the basic things like the stories, dream time stories. Because me, our uncle, Rich, my dad brother, he had all the story, all the dream time stories and tell about the gobble dreaming and the sister rocks and all that.
And then we had to go into, he sent us down to Uncle Bill, Uncle Bill Congo. And we went down there and he taught us how to paint in his way, see? And we learned by his way. And that's how eventually the story has started to develop as a concept of children's storybook.
For the people. And also we had Bill Blackley, who was also a teacher at Palm Island State School. We called it State School before, but today they call it Bullgerman School. And he used to be my teacher too, also Bill. And he also brought all the stories together and...
And develop it and recreate it into a story which was created by my dad. I call it dad because it's my uncle and my father. And then that's how it all started out and sort of kept me going. And by the time when I left then I went to college, did some artworks up there.
Sort of grew on me and started using different style of artworks like using screen printing, batiks and also lino printing.
And we do some bit of works on campus and then we do a lot of traveling and selling them. I was at the Cairns College of TAFE back in, I think it was 1980s, 82, 83, 1983. And then from there, it was there, then I went up to Northern Territory then and to Kasserina University and did my diploma of fine arts.
And from there, I would stay there for five years. When I got my graduate diploma of fine arts, they asked for a student to go down to Melbourne, the RMIT. I went down for a student residency and worked with the students in RMIT.
Teach them our culture through there. And what I learned from there, printing, lino prints and all that, etchings. And I stayed there until three, four, five years now. Another five years. And then as I'd done all that, I was pretty good at that and came back to Palm. I was a bit homesick, I think.
The weather was down, it was cold. And when I left Darwin, Northern Territory, it was hot. And then I went down to the cold area. Sort of different sort of way. And when I look at it, you know, new life.
What did it feel like? Did you feel like you were always representing your culture and your place in all of those places when you were doing your art?
Like how did you learn technique that then matched with your cultural?
Well, yeah. Well, basically with different, with a technique like a lino print, it's just so you're not using a knife, using a brush, you're also using a pen, using a knife. Then you have to cut the material and to carve out the image that you want to put on the lino print.
On the lino, then you use Indian ink, then you roll it on top of it, then you put it through a press. It's like a press, you know, what a press does when they do printing for newspapers and all that. It's sort of different. This is an idea, but it goes in a different perspective, like back to front, but it goes the right way we wanted it.
So you have to line it up, and roll it through and then the next step you get to start, you get the first stage, you gotta use six different colors, overlay different color layers of colors, ink, Indian ink, and it's very, very good too. It keeps me going.
What is it about art that made you want to do it? Was it to tell a story? Was it to represent your culture?
Well, you know, arts always said, all this arts is coming to be something that's more creative in your mind, in your mind that you want to create something. So like wood carving, you want to make...
Carve out a dugong on the wood. So you carve, it's how you create, how you create that image. In an art, it's a flowing thing. It's an expression. It sort of gives you the reality of what you see and what you know. And then you can sort of use the brush as you, as a...
As your heart and your mind take you to it and you create something. Aboriginal art, it's unique.
Are you comfortable talking me through, you showed me an artwork at the hospital and you had a snake.
Yeah.
Are you comfortable talking through that and what the story is?
The story there that when we tell the story of that, that when I done at the hospital with the Gabul dreaming, see? So it was the snake that came down from Herbert River, came all the way down and he came all the way down and he...
And broke into pieces and then he came through and went up that way and landed on and came down that way to see where he came to Palm, made his way to Palm and then...
And then we came to a water hole with bamboo cricks. And that snake lays there. And then the old family said, no, you can't go up there. Tell the daughters not to go up there swimming. You're not allowed to go up there swimming. But they went up and then went for a swim there.
And then the snake took them all the way up. That way he ran all the way up to, going up to Mount Bentley, all the way around. And then the Gabul snake came down to, they call it, Barbara Bay. And there you got, you have Gabul Snake Creek there. And the land, it was all water, no water was there.
Crawled all the way up to a place called Mad Daddy Garland and he went to Mad Daddy. The old man, the old father, he was a clever man too. And he trailed, he followed the tracks all the way and went all the way all over. And he came down to Gabul Snake Creek where the snake went through. Then today there, you go around there,
And then you see that creek there still running. It's called the Carpacini Creek, around where Barbara Bay is, and then Osho Bay there, in between there. And it went all the way over to Magnetic. And then they found him there, found him there.
He asked, that Gabul snake didn’t ask him not to kill him. And he said, take the daughter, take the girl and brought her back. And he didn’t want to kill the snake, so the snake, he said, he let the snake go. And he went, grabbed the girl and went back to Palm. And the girl was sick, so the old man just healed her.
Today and today, you see that when he go, that Gabul snake, he let him go because he went up to the Ross River and he created the Ross River and that was it. That’s the whole story connected.
Why did that story sort of connect you to you and why did you end up painting it? Was there a reason or was it just a feeling?
Well, the Gabul, it’s a totem. And it’s a story connection to country, and the dreaming, and the connection with our dreamings connected to the island. The same as the creator, he created all these islands too, also.
When he came then, all the way from, came across to Herbert River, he came through Herbert, came down to Herbert, created that Herbert River, then came through it, and all the way landed and came to Palm. And from there, he went over there to Magnetic, and Magnetic went straight up to and created Ross River. And the story, and it's come back again to us.
And it’s connected with us too, with our dreaming, with Gabul dreaming. And it also gives us the thoughts that we’re here with Herbert River. It’s where all that area, it’s where we all come down with descendants and families. We come from up Tableland all the way down and to Palm and the connection there and all over too.
And that’s why, that’s why Dad or grandfather would always say, we’re under the umbrella of the Rukurrukaba country.
Ukurukaba, this oldest big area that we cover under, we are called Kunu people. Ukurukaba means Kunu people. It’s very special. Yeah, it’s a little special. And we also associate with Banyan, Hinchinbrook Banyan.
Nowagi, over that side, Waihingum and all that area. And also come down to Rukurrukaba, Ulkuru and Bindal, all that area there. And all this connection has come under the umbrella of Rukurrukaba country. We’re all Kunu people.
How do new people come onto the island and understand that? Like the complexity and the simplicity of that? How do you best welcome people, I guess, in the right way, and how can people come in the right way?
We welcome them and sometimes we go, we take them, when they come, we take them around the way, the casement there where the story tree is. We do a smoking ceremony, we welcome them and bring them into the country so that they can also be protected from bad spirits. And let them enjoy themselves on Palm and welcome them on Great Palm itself.
Bukkuman Parah. Bukkuman Parah means Great Palm Island and welcome them all over. Everyone over Great Palm and enjoy themselves. And they go back.
What’s the... I don’t know what the question is, but... Palm’s been through a journey of many things.
Yeah, Palm’s been through a lot. You get... you get... you get Benedict, like, strikes. Hundred years celebration. And... and... Bookman holidays, you know.
And you also have the memories of our brother, Peter Fry, who would tell the stories of having shot curry. And that’s a respect for... that’s the story that, his stories, and it’s still celebrated today.
And respected. That’s how we give them the opportunity to show their respect, and we show our respect. And that’s how we show our respect.
How do you think about yourself around some of the tougher times that have happened on Palm Island?
You think about it, and it’s part of the journey, or is it something in which, like, happened but you need to move on? Like, what’s the... how do you feel about what happened back in the time?
Sometimes I’m not too sure, you know. Life’s...
People want to live in a beautiful tropical island. It’s beautiful, but the responsibility, we go back in the time, we look at it. When you go back under the Act, when you look at the old pictures, old photos, beautify that island, it’s all clean. And it’s just like that. We’ve been under the Act, see?
We were like prisoners, and we showed that we cleaned places up. But when the Act was gone, we were free. We can do what we like. We’ll do what we can. And the purpose is that we can’t change. We’ve got to go forward and try to develop and sometimes move on.
And there’s also a time for celebration. And I don’t know. There’s some amazing things happening on Palm Island. There’s some tough things as well that people are working through.
What’s some of the things that you hope will happen over the next maybe like 10 to 20 years on Palm? Are there things in which you’re hopeful about?
I want to remember that, hopefully, that everybody be all together as one and work together and respect each other and celebrate what we can. Keep Palm... keep Palm beautiful and keep going ahead, going ahead in the future. And that’s what I look at.
But for myself, I like to develop something for myself and bring something. Maybe we can, because Palm's going to be around when they have tourism coming,
People that we need to work in and develop, you know, business and all that on Palm. So I want to try and do something for... have a little place for where we can bring young people back into culture, learning things that are, that are vulnerable at Palm.
I think culture is most important. People will stay focused on things that happened back there, but history...
Can repeat itself, you know. But we got to go, we got to use every resource that our culture will go forward and keep it with our young generation coming up. And nobody with a telephone or mobile phones in this beautiful place where this whole inspiration is all around us. Everything’s here.
So you told me a really inspiring vision yesterday.
Yeah, I was going to bring it up one day.
I’d love for you to...
Talk through what that vision is.
I was saying that I was talking about it, trying to bring it out and trying to bring it so I can explain it.
I felt the segue was good.
Yeah, try to bring it in and try to explain it, how I’m going to do it.
Yeah.
I was there last night. We should have talked about it.
But you’re going to start working, is it on?
I’ll edit it.
Yeah.
I can ask you specific questions about it.
Well, I was looking at North East Bay, and I was trying to think of that I was going to do that just to make it a little camping place for young kids and kids that seek...
I’m thinking of a word that might bring it up in a language name, but it’s "seek and you shall find."
And it sort of creates culture in perspective, where you can see it or believe it or you don’t. It’s up whether it’s with your heart, whether you want it to happen.
Culture is most important. That’s why I want to create this camping, so that maybe they don’t go to school, maybe they like to, but education comes first.
And also, culture brings in the... I don’t know, it’s just, it’s what I’m thinking of. I’m trying to bring it in a picture where I can make it happen, but it’s...
Some other people help, you know, like teachers, police, or whoever can be involved with it too, you know, more creative.
But it’s most important—culture first. Culture.
Can you explain like where it is and why that place is significant, do you think, for where you want it to be?
Lorde’s Bay is beautiful. It’s quiet.
The beach, the water, and also it has everything there. You just have your mind thinking back and start bringing people, bringing culture back into it.
Camping, walking back, walkabout, bush walking,
Go seek other places and story connection too, connecting and hunting and fishing. It’s all that part of culture. We get to learn to hunt, you get to feed yourself, you get to learn to say go into the store or shops.
Maybe now I’ll try to check everything out. That’s why I wanted to start up my vision. It’s a vision I always use because it’s away from everything.
And it was isolated there. You know, also comfort and quietness.
Yeah.
Also, you can do your paintings and all that, and art, and create, make some shields or spears or create something.
And it brings you back to...
Brings you back to reality with culture that you want to do. And it’s what you want to do to help you go forward, to help you be more a person.
And what do you think that does for a young person who is currently struggling a little bit with the system and school and stuff? Why does that experience help them, do you think?
I know I’ve been there at school. I was struggling. I learned a few, my English and mainly my maths, but it wasn’t helping much. But it’s just looking, just that you’ve got to try harder.
Put yourself, work harder, try to, and focus on, maybe you could get some friends around the school, help you out, keep encouraging you, parents encourage you if you need it, teachers are there too, if they need it, friends there, if you need it. All they gotta do is just...
And what difference do you think having strong elders to be able to talk to makes for young people? And like how do you, with a place like that, how do you...?
Culturally, like I go back to culture and then see your Palm, you have 40 different, 40 or 30 different tribes on the island, and each of them come from a different country, see? Different places where they come, because they come under the umbrella of Bulgaman people, and they're 32 different tribes, and as a young generation, each will have to seek and find where their connections are.
We’re not gonna say we’re gonna send you away back up there. You’re free to go up there back to your grandfather’s country and come back. That’s how you generate yourself to be who you really are, who you’re connected to, where your connections are. And you also go there to visit your families and your relatives.
And say that, oh, my grandfather’s name was there. I was back to my grandfather’s country and come back to Palm because in that way, that sort of builds you up, see? So you know who you are. Where I come from, I got my mother, my mother is a Giribau.
She’s up in Madagascar. Madagascar is a whole new country. My mother and grandmother, they all worked at the station. They worked at a station called Kunawara. Kunawara Station. And then we go out there, but our grandfather, my mother, my mother’s dad, grandmother, grandmother, she said that Baja Balanar changed it to...
Kirama Station, changing to Bajabala Station, which means "two rivers meet." And it’s almost not far from where the Blinko Falls are. They went up there, Mount Garnet area, that side. And that’s where the Blinko Falls, that’s where Warrung Country and Guggenbaden, yeah.
And that’s where my mother’s country is, up that way, Tableland. And then I come back down here where Dad’s country is Mumbara. And here we go, Boogerman Burra. Boogerman Burra is Great Palm Island and Mumbara.
So how long was this?
We’re doing good. We’re going to beat Richard.
Oh my God, I’m going to get so bummed.
Yeah, I know.
36 minutes, all right.
Long, isn’t it?
You’re so good.
Oh, now you got to break it up and make sure it comes to the old meat. I want to look at it, see where anything goes wrong. I got to make sure.
Oh, yeah. That’s the best part.
We need to, we need to, we need to, we got to correct it first.
I didn’t want to.
Yeah.
What do you think young fellas’ journey through this life is like? I don’t know if it’s expectation or there’s something around understanding your culture, but then they’ve got this other world, this Western-type construct that they need to work out.
How do they do that? Like, is that something that... Do you think that’s why some young people are struggling so much?
Yeah. When you have these sort of things like, you know, back in the old days, we used to go walk up and look around for fruit, you know, look around for cherry trees and plums and all that, back in those days.
We used to go down the jetty, get some oysters. Then at the beachside, get some oysters. These were the good times back in those days.
And we, you know, we walk about, we free walkabout and then take our spear, go spearfishing, go fishing, you know, around the bay and all that.
But the next generation, when the time, it’s all been changed because they lack, lack of this because of mobile phones are coming around and...
Americanized and they talking like American, as the gangsters, and talking like, and I said, oh, you’re not American, you’re bloody Aboriginal.
Where’s you?
You get mobile phones and you get all kinds of things. You get scooters, you get things that are made today, but back in our days...
All we had was a little foot. We walked around like we used to always do.
But now these days, it’s slowly, but sometimes we have to try and change, but it’s not.
Sometimes also religion plays a game in all our life too. Religion, churches. But church is good. It helps. I’m not religious, but I’m a Christian. I believe in God, you know.
But I also wanted to show that our first priority is to believe the way what we believe, you know. Either you want to be what you want to be. You know, we make our choices.
But then again, we’ve got cultural perspective too, and it might combine, but, you know...
We use it as what God has shown us to use it the right way. And not to kill one another. And, you know, we live as a peaceful people.
But I’m talking about back in the time, see, when we were all, when we had this freedom of going hunting...
Get some cherry trees or get some plums. And guava, there was the days when we had that.
But now, when we go back to mobile phones and all that, we change all that. TV, telephones, even shopping used to go out there.
We used to go to the shop all the time and push the trolley.
Now, it’s all that. You drive a car.
You can’t walk anymore, you get too used to the car, because, oh, I’m getting too lazy now. I need to drive a car.
And it’s all changing.
We used to go out to the camping, we used to carry a little bag with blankets and all that.
But now you’ve got a caravan coming around and you can use a caravan.
You could get a tent and they could make a tent.
We used to make them all, a little old hut and camp underneath it.
But now everything’s changed, young generation.
But it also, protections, that’s all it needs, your protection and your health.
What do you think’s going to change?
I’d rather be back there, but now you’ve got to go forward now and make the best of it.
But still believe in what you can do for the young generation.
First thing first.
Make sure they get back, first priority is their culture first.
And maybe they can...
Sit down and talk about what they do. You could use your mobile phone, but put it away.
Then you can come and we’ll go walkabout, camp, and bring your mobile phone along, take photos of what we’re doing, see?
You create something. And sharing with culture, what you can create your mobile phone to do. And make sure that you sort of keep a continuation of history, of what you’ve been doing. And people say, oh, this is Bush Tucker. Take a photo. And that keeps it in there. It’s like your memory.
There are some kids that end up getting caught up in this. There’s a system called youth justice or youth detention. Is there an alternative to that that you can offer in the Palm Island community that helps those young people to change and understand how to live without committing crime or getting in trouble? Or do they have to go to prison?
Well, things are going out of line sometimes, you know. We try our best. But focus back on the parents. Parents have a responsibility. And also, kids can do all kinds of things the wrong way.
Just growing up, you know. Growing up. That’s all it is. Growing up too fast. Not slowing them down. Meet them on the right track. Make sure they go where they...
Expect to be, not expect to be, to go where you want them to go. But it’s all about... I don’t know how you could put it. I haven’t got a kid of my own, but I just got my nephews and my niece and grandchildren.
Would be my brothers and sisters. And try to keep them in the right direction and make sure they stay on that. And also mainly because when you go back in the old ways, you’ve got to have that respect. Family respect. You respect your elders. You respect your elders and you respect...
You respect your mother, you respect your father, you respect your brother, and also the families around you. The most important is your elders. You must respect your elders.
Back in the old days, if you don’t listen, listen and hear, listen to what they say, you get a clip over the ears. You do the wrong thing, you get a clip over the ears.
But nowadays, kids can do what they like now. But even it’s up to ourselves, we can make a change, we can change it. We can use every resource that brings them...
Bring that respect back into the families, bring it back into the kids and all that. Your elders come first.
Yeah.
If over the next few years Palm Island starts to develop tourism as well...
The gentleman, he’s seen us out here. He’s checking us out.
Yeah, he was standing there looking.
Was he?
Yeah.
He said, what are you doing here?
No way I’m getting out of here. There’s someone down there.
Sure.
Yeah, we just got a visit over the horse. He got up and just came and visited us. He wanted to join in the interview.
Sorry about that.
If Palm Island in the next five or ten years starts to develop tourism and more people start to come, what would you hope that they take away or that they...
Feel when they’re here? What are the things that you think are most important for them?
Well, it’s most important that Palm can give, what Palm can provide, and Palm can produce. Tourism can be the opportunity for themselves to develop themselves and become a...
Whatever they expect it to be. You know, like more money, more work. We have more people working, more Wulgurukaba people, more people working together to develop something. And when tourists come, they want to see culture.
It’s the first priority. They want to see what Palm can produce, what Palm can have. Say, maybe we can have a dancing group. Maybe we can have a camping group.
Maybe we can have tourism for looking at the Mingna Mingna Ranges to develop the tourist brand all over, everywhere, and touring up the hill. Mingna Mingna Ranges can control the sea and the land also.
And also mainly to come back to respect the traditional owners and also the people here too, also respected as the Wulgurukaba people. And Mambara also to be a first priority.
And we wanted to go forward and bring everybody forward with us, work together.
Can you see the bay down here if you walk up there or not?
Up here?
Yeah.
We can walk up.
Can you see it?
Yeah.
Oh, my leg. I’m going to jump on that horseback.
Oh, get up.

\# Uncle Allan Welcome

\*\*Speaker 3:\*\* [00:00:00] Good morning, everyone. My name is Alan Palm Island. We are here on Spoongeman Barra, Great Palm Island, and Daru Maru. We look around Great Palm, all the rest of the islands around the surrounding islands. And we are here today to learn about myself. My skin name is Nakawaraka, skin name. And our language name, our language is Mulkal.

And we speak in, in, in our town that that we, we speak our language, that we call Nakarawaraka Burbanbara. You're welcome to Great Palm. But I say that Bougamambara. Bougamambara means Great Palm Island, Mambara, and Darumaru [00:01:00] means the rest of the islands or surrounding islands of palm, Great Palm.

Today we just wanted to say that the islands behind me, it's Nuru, but they call it Curacao. Nuruwapri, North Palm, and Bougambarin. And across here, we got Guggenbeiren is Hofje's Island and you got across over here to Emilia, which is Fannum Island. Palm, Great Palm is, is sitting on as we got here on our emblem is, is Mingina Mingina Ranges.

And in this, in this emblem emblem, we have a, what we call a shield. We call Bukal. Bukal means shield. And we. We, we put, I [00:02:00] put the designs on it as a two, because our boundary is, is, is come into form of a, of a big Mandaray. Our boundary, we call it Mingina Mingina Ranges, Mingina Mingina, Mingina Mingina.

Our boundaries is that area of Great Palm Island. And in, in that area, it would keep, and I'm just trying to welcome you all today. Thanks for coming.

storyteller.bio: Uncle Alan Palm Island is a Traditional Owner Director for the Manbarra people and accomplished artist whose life bridges ancient cultural knowledge with contemporary artistic expression. With the skin name Nakawaraka and totem Kurenja (stingray), Uncle Alan learned traditional arts from his father before pursuing formal education at Cairns TAFE, Katherine University, and RMIT Melbourne, where he earned graduate qualifications in fine arts while teaching Aboriginal culture to students. A master storyteller particularly known for the Gabul (snake) dreaming story that connects Palm Island to the broader Wulgurukaba country, he currently leads the Mingna Mingna Rangers and holds a powerful vision for establishing a cultural camping site at North East Bay where young people can reconnect with traditional ways of living. His philosophy of "culture first" emphasizes that before youth can navigate contemporary challenges, they must understand their identity through connection to country, traditional practices, and respect for elders, while his approach to future tourism development prioritizes cultural authenticity and traditional owner rights.

storyteller.bio: Richard Cassidy is an Indigenous leader and mentor who bridges traditional cultural knowledge with contemporary community development on Palm Island. As a program director focused on ranger operations and leadership development, he works to empower young people through cultural education, environmental stewardship, and professional skills training while maintaining deep connections to country and traditional ways of being. Drawing from both Indigenous law and mainstream systems, Richard guides his team with wisdom and authenticity, helping them navigate multiple worlds while building capacity and creating positive change in their community.

I can just say white cockatoo is my dreaming clan group and it's situated at Philip Creek and it's a dreaming site we follow from start to finish. And there's another one that I'm connected through. The white cockatoo is the the Yukoorla. The Spinifex works.. And we make bush medicine out of Yukoorla and it's really good stuff. Tennent Creek is a small [00:01:00] community town which has different language groups here.

So everyone knows everyone. And if new people in town, we could just ask someone and say, oh, that's, that person is connected to that family group.

We have an Aboriginal organisation, which we are trying to set up Wilya Janta. We're trying to set up that one for housing and we're trying to start with our house. Culturally appropriate way. We're designing it to go with the, our culture fits in with our climate as well.

It's climate friendly, house.

We are hoping to do that with tourists to do cultural awareness within our language groups. And within our country, and to teach people who wants to know about our language and culture and our living environment and our languages, what's here.

[00:00:00] isolation is like the struggle of modern society, then connection to communities, the antidote.

I think it's practical. It's practical, more so than anything. It's awesome. Also it speaks to what people that are living on the streets need in a wider sense is access to facilities . There's two types of facilities that would benefit from having community access to the first is necessary.

Utilities like kitchen, shower, laundry. 'cause there aren't spaces where you can just go to do those necessary living function things for free. And the second, third space that would be amazing to see more so in the community is free spaces just to be and to build community from, for example a clothing exchange, like free clothing exchange, [00:01:00] a place with couches, with a kitchen, with a lounge, just to hang out during the daytime.

A place where there's a free bookshelf, a place that encourages free trade. 'cause if you can facilitate an environment where people can help people, that's the best way to solve things. Most people are generous especially people that are in difficult situations.

stories.title: Coping with grief
stories.content:
\# Robyn Watts

[00:00:00] 

Robin Watts. You want to know my life story? Okay. Got two girls. I started out life as a teacher, working life as a teacher.

Didn't like that and got a job in local government, so I ended up the last job I had there for 20 years. And then after I retired, I discovered orange sky and my husband got sick. And he subsequently died. And Orange Sky, as I've told Nic, saved me. It made me get out of bed every day, try and push through the grief, and it's just been the best thing I've ever done, apart from having a lovely family.

Oh, I love it. I just absolutely love it. I honestly believe. [00:01:00] That we give a lot to friends, but they give just as much back. I go home on top of the world some days. Yeah. And I look forward to the days that I'm on shift. I love it. Really love it.

It was compounded, my husband had myeloma and the life expectancy of myeloma now is seven years, and he died after about. Three and a half. So he didn't last very long. But grief for my husband dying was a second wave of grief because six weeks before he died, our 42-year-old son-in-law just died suddenly in Sydney, leaving a 4-year-old and a 6-year-old.

And my daughter. And totally unexpected, just completely out of left field. And he was the most wonderful human being. He was [00:02:00] American. And then later on, Ron died. And that was, I think I no, I was in denial of how sick he was. Every time we went to the hematologist, I would. Feel, oh, it wasn't that bad.

It could have been worse, but something happened to his spleen and he just said one night, I feel like I've got a pain in my chest. So I thought it might have been a heart. His heart went into hospital, didn't come out. And ended up in ICU for a week, which was horrible. Horrible. And then went into palliative care and died the next day.

So it was, but he had also been an orange sky volunteer, so I felt like I was carrying on the family tradition too by continuing to do that. But it truly did help me get out of bed. I had to, I had no choice. People depending on you, and without that, I [00:03:00] probably could have stayed. But everybody I know has said to me how well I've coped.

And I think I've coped reasonably well. But I, I miss him. Of course .

I do on my shift on Thursday, we've got, that's the longest shift we've had.

It's the oldest shift and we, the team, I've got the two boys I volunteer with, we've been together for years, probably five years. Or Russ has probably been there nearly seven years. And yes, they were supportive. I was very touched that the team leaders all went to Ron's funeral. Very unexpected. And they've helped me a lot.

But the interesting thing was that the friends. Where my shift on Thursday is the friends knew him too. That was nice, there was a consistency there. But I just I just love it. Absolutely love it. Are there particular things about it that you think are [00:04:00] more profound than others or because I think there's some parts of the, so just simple, but some parts thought out. I think it's, yes, the laundry's important obviously for. People's dignity and they have a right to that. But I think making them feel seen and heard, for me personally, that's really important and genuinely, calling them by name and remembering to ask them something.

One of my favorite quotes is from Maya Angelou says, people will forget what you said, forget what you did. But they will never forget the way you made them feel. And I really believe that. I think that is true for me, but I try to make that true for them too. So I'll, we'll talk about something that's meaningful to them.

I think one of the trickier things is learning to respect and know the [00:05:00] boundaries because some people don't wanna share that much. And we've got a friend who we would, we are very frustrated. We really wanna be able to help him, but he feels that he has enough and he doesn't want to take anymore.

And he struggles, but I've since found out he has got an advocate, which is really good. But that's a failing in the system. I think this particular friend is quite deaf and he's waited probably 18 months to get hearing aids, and I don't know how much they've shown him, but we had a volunteer on the shift one day who'd had some experience as an audiologist.

So she showed him how to put them in and he said, oh, I can hear now, but I don't, he's not doing it himself and we can't offer he's quite private. And he's quite proud, which we respect.

I'm up to my nine years this year, and I wanna get my 10 years, then I'll get my unpaid long service leave.

No, I just, that is [00:06:00] a very concrete goal. I want to get to my 10 years. I've got no intention of leaving at this stage. Sometimes some of the processes that come from HQ can be a bit frustrating. I have to say though, I'd like this on record that my regional coordinator, Carolyn, is superb.

She is the best I've ever worked with. She is just amazing. Her level of support to me as service leader is immeasurable. So she's a buffer between me and the powers that be.

They didn't put ours in last year. They forgot it. And that's, I know I get that we are one of however many services in Australia, but to us we are the service in Tassie. So that sort of thing upsets me a little bit.

stories.title: Empathy Over Judgment: Seeing the Person, Not Just the Addiction
stories.content:
Empathy Over Judgment: Seeing the Person, Not Just the Addiction
===

Briget Perry: ~If they notice somebody's on drugs, is there a way to feel more comfortable and not be just immediately scared and think, oh no, that's a scary drug addict. Like they're people too. ~[00:00:00] They use drugs. Yes. But they need to be seen as people just like everybody else.

So I really like there to be some sort of harm reduction awareness training for volunteers in Canberra.

Having service providers to partner with is a really smart way of doing things because it's not just we park the van and that's it. Like we park the van and we have Vinny's come, or we're at. Red Cross Roadhouse or early morning Center where they're serving food or whatever it is.

It's not just the one thing, it's we've partnered with someone else and that's the business model and it's smart. So I think always expanding and thinking of how you can expand the service that little bit farther is really smart.

It's just a matter of, trying to get HQ and the service [00:01:00] volunteer here and all of that stuff. All the pieces put in the right places. I've been trying, I've been trying to do it.

~When I started, a volunteer that was on shift with me had said that somebody asked her, oh, that's great that you're volunteering your time, but like, why not just give them money?~

storyteller.bio: Freddy Wai is a resilient refugee from Papua New Guinea who received asylum in Australia in 2024, bringing with him deep insights about human rights, community connection, and personal growth. Despite facing significant challenges including homelessness and cultural adjustment, he maintains an optimistic perspective and deep appreciation for Australia's beauty and the support services available to those in need. Freddy's story exemplifies courage and perseverance as he works to build a new life while holding onto his cultural heritage, and he aspires to give back to his community through volunteer work once he feels more established.

storytellers.bio: Benjamin Knight is deeply inspired by Diagrama’s nurturing approach to youth detention. Reflecting on his experiences, he contrasts the positive educational environment of Diagrama with harsher detention models, driving his vision for broad-scale transformative youth justice practices.

Shaun Fisher, an Eastern Aboriginal oyster farmer on North Stradbroke Island, is leading a movement to reclaim Indigenous economic sovereignty through commercial oyster farming. By combining traditional tripod methods with modern techniques, he's building generational wealth for his community while challenging existing power structures in the industry through collective action and a First Nations Oyster Growers Association.

Peggy Palm Island is a traditional owner of Palm Island from the Mambarra tribe and an Indigenous elder. One of nine siblings (four sisters and five brothers), she has lived on Palm Island most of her life. She joined the rangers program at the encouragement of her nephew Alan and helps preserve cultural knowledge, including the significant "Three Sisters" dreamtime story about women who drowned and turned to stone. Peggy is passionate about reconnecting young people with their cultural heritage and keeping them "on the straight and narrow."

Gary champions Men’s Shed initiatives focusing on woodworking, community mental health, skill-building for youth, and practical solutions addressing homelessness. His holistic approach emphasizes empowerment through cultural connection and community collaboration.

Kate Bjur serves as the Executive Director for Research and Advocacy at Peak Care in Queensland, bringing extensive experience from education, child protection, and youth justice sectors. Following her Churchill Fellowship investigating youth detention models internationally, Kate was profoundly impacted by her visit to Diagrama in Spain, where she witnessed approaches dramatically different from Australian practices.

Benjamin Knight is deeply inspired by Diagrama’s nurturing approach to youth detention. Reflecting on his experiences, he contrasts the positive educational environment of Diagrama with harsher detention models, driving his vision for broad-scale transformative youth justice practices.
A group of young men from Murcia, Spain, who support each other through life's challenges and demonstrate resilience in the face of uncertainty.

Javier Aparicio Grau is dedicated to nurturing youth through structured, activity-rich daily routines. His extensive experience ensures a nurturing environment emphasizing personal growth and recreational enrichment.

Young People Murcia represents a community of youth in Spain who are actively engaged in personal growth and development through supportive educational programs. Through their experiences, they demonstrate resilience and aspiration, engaging thoughtfully with topics ranging from career ambitions to cultural exchange, while benefiting from Spain's progressive approach to youth development that emphasizes education and rehabilitation. Their perspectives offer valuable insights into the importance of meaningful adult-youth relationships and the positive impact of comprehensive support systems in fostering youth potential.

Marillie Giannakopoulou serves as Operations Coordinator at Europe's first mobile laundry unit in Greece, where she manages both the facility and its employees who come from vulnerable backgrounds. With a degree in International Relations and minor in Psychology, she is passionate about providing dignity through clean clothes and hygiene services to homeless individuals while helping staff members reintegrate into society. Marillie oversees the multipurpose center's daily operations with empathy and dedication, working to raise global awareness about the fundamental importance of laundry access for human dignity and social inclusion.

Dimitra Kountourioti serves as Director of Ithaca, a mobile laundry service in Athens providing dignity and clean clothes to people experiencing homelessness. Starting as the organization's first employee in 2017, she has grown the operation from a single van to include comprehensive social services while advocating for policy changes to expand access. Through her leadership, Dimitra works to challenge stereotypes, create safe spaces for vulnerable populations, and establish hygiene as a fundamental human right, all while building global partnerships to enhance impact across communities.

Melissa Jackson is a community member and mother from the Top End region of Australia who has called Tennant Creek home since she was five years old. Living with her extended family, including her son and relatives, she appreciates Tennant Creek for its tight-knit community where "everyone knows each other" and its ability to bring new opportunities to residents. Melissa's authentic perspective on her hometown highlights its value as a "bright place" that fosters connection across generations, from supporting youth activities to meeting the needs of elders in the community.

Chloe, an Aboriginal Homeless Fringe Support Worker, actively advocates for practical and innovative solutions to improve the harsh living conditions of homeless communities, addressing immediate health risks and fostering collaborative stakeholder engagement.

Daniel Patrick Noble is a visitor to Palm Island from Yarrabah, near Cairns. He has strong family connections to Palm Island through his aunt who has lived there since her high school days, and he completed Year 5 of his schooling on the island. Daniel describes Palm Island as feeling "like home" due to his extended family connections and the fact that "a lot of people know me" there.

Dianne Stokes is a traditional owner who has lived on her ancestral land for 23 years, initially residing in her car before establishing more permanent shelter. Her land holds profound personal significance, with Dianne describing a spiritual connection that calls her back whenever she is away, providing a sense of freedom and cultural continuity.

Gloria is a dialysis patient originally from Warburton who relocated to Kalgoorlie for ongoing treatment. Having grown up in the Christian community of Cosmo, she now manages her health condition while maintaining connections with family members who provide essential support during her treatment journey.

Annie Morrison grew up on Rocking Dam station in the 1960s before attending Euro College in 1982. She later returned to her grandfather's country, establishing a homeland approximately 87 kilometers from Tennent Creek. Annie values her indigenous heritage and aims to pass traditional practices to the next generation.

Jimmy Frank is a respected Indigenous cultural leader and community advocate from Tennant Creek, Northern Territory, with deep connections to both Warumungu and Western Arrernte country through his parents' lineages. Drawing from his early experiences learning traditional practices from elders, he has dedicated his career to cultural preservation and community development, serving as a cultural liaison officer and chairperson of Willgunya Housing Project while actively working to challenge stereotypes and empower Aboriginal voices in housing, health and social initiatives. Through his involvement with traditional dance, ceremony, and the Brio artists group, Jimmy champions Indigenous-led decision making and works to ensure Aboriginal knowledge and culture remain central to community solutions.

Patricia Frank is a Warmonger woman from Nan Creek who balances her cultural identity with community service through her work at an Aboriginal health corporation. With intimate knowledge of Tenant Creek's diverse language groups and community dynamics, she advocates for culturally appropriate housing and tourism initiatives while maintaining deep connections to her clan group traditions.

Linda Turner, known as LT for cultural reasons regarding the use of deceased people's names, is a proud indigenous woman born 160 kilometers north of Tennent Creek in the 1960s. Having spent her first 13 years growing up on a cattle station in the bush, Linda reflects on the positive communal aspect of her childhood while expressing concern about current cultural losses and the ongoing impacts of the Intervention on Aboriginal communities.

Jenni Calcraft is the station manager at Orpheus Island Research Station owned by James Cook University. A marine biologist who grew up in Brisbane, she now lives and works on Orpheus/Gullbody Island. Jenni is passionate about increasing women's participation in marine science, particularly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women. She serves as a facilitator for ocean activities and helps document culturally significant underwater sites, including the "Three Sisters" rocks at East Palm Island.

Jess Smit has lived in Townsville for 18 years with a background in education. She currently serves as the project officer for the ATSIMS program, which engages First Nations high school students in marine science. Her career began teaching on Palm Island, giving her long-standing connections with community members. Jess is dedicated to capacity building and empowering others, particularly through marine experiences, and sees herself continuing to work with Palm Island in different capacities over time.

Allison Paley is an American-born marine scientist who moved to Australia about 20 years ago and is now an Australian citizen and mother to Aboriginal children. She coordinates the AT-SIMS (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders in Marine Science) program at James Cook University, collaborating with the Mumba Elders Council and Minga Minga Rangers. Allison is passionate about experiential education outside the classroom and supporting Indigenous women in marine science. She values the importance of listening to and recording cultural stories from elders.

Paige Tanner Hill is an 18-year-old from Palm Island who recently graduated from Bwgcolman Community School and now works as a junior ranger. She participated in diving at the culturally significant "Two Sisters" reef and helps lead tours about Palm Island's history, including the Stolen Generation. Paige aspires to become a marine biologist or scientist and recognizes the importance of connecting with her culture and sharing these stories with other Palm Islanders.

Peggy Palm Island is a traditional owner of Palm Island from the Mambarra tribe and an Indigenous elder. One of nine siblings (four sisters and five brothers), she has lived on Palm Island most of her life. She joined the rangers program at the encouragement of her nephew Alan and helps preserve cultural knowledge, including the significant "Three Sisters" dreamtime story about women who drowned and turned to stone. Peggy is passionate about reconnecting young people with their cultural heritage and keeping them "on the straight and narrow."

Benjamin Moss is a Senior Lecturer at the University of Queensland's Moreton Bay Research Station, where he leads teaching and research initiatives in marine sciences with a focus on oyster reef restoration and habitat preservation. As the first full-time academic based at the station, he works closely with Indigenous Elders and community members to integrate traditional knowledge with scientific research, creating sustainable solutions for marine conservation and community development. Through programs like the Deadly Marine Science Days, Moss demonstrates his commitment to fostering educational opportunities that bridge scientific understanding with Indigenous wisdom, while supporting the development of First Nations businesses and environmental stewardship.

Tarren fosters cultural identity and healing through ancestral ceremonies. His engagement with youth at graveyard flower ceremonies promotes cultural pride and emotional healing, addressing intergenerational trauma.

Shaun Fisher, an Eastern Aboriginal oyster farmer on North Stradbroke Island, is leading a movement to reclaim Indigenous economic sovereignty through commercial oyster farming. By combining traditional tripod methods with modern techniques, he's building generational wealth for his community while challenging existing power structures in the industry through collective action and a First Nations Oyster Growers Association.

Patricia Ann Miller, AO, a proud traditional owner, is renowned for her extensive service in community and legal sectors. Holding two doctorates, she’s interacted with international dignitaries, contributing significantly to cultural and administrative leadership for over two decades.

Tanya Turner, an Eastern Aboriginal woman from Central Australia, pursued law instead of acting despite her drama teacher's objections. After working in Melbourne's Supreme Court as the first Indigenous associate, she returned to Alice Springs to serve her community, moving from debt recovery to Aboriginal legal aid where she found fulfillment providing community legal education while addressing systemic justice issues.

Kristy is a community leader passionate about fostering partnerships and projects that support Indigenous youth and families. Actively involved in developing culturally significant walking trails, she emphasizes shared knowledge and collaboration between diverse communities like Napa Homestead and Palm Island.

Margot Scales is a dedicated Orange Sky volunteer who began her service after retiring at age 75 from a career that included working at Parliament. As part of a close-knit Monday morning shift team in Hobart, Tasmania, she brings warmth, humor and compassionate listening to her interactions with community members experiencing homelessness. Margot's commitment to creating meaningful connections while providing practical laundry services exemplifies her belief in the power of casual, judgment-free support to make a difference in people's lives.

Nicole Snead serves as a Core Officer at the Salvation Army in Hobart, Tasmania, where she has dedicated 18 years to full-time ministry alongside her husband John. Drawing from her lifelong connection to the Salvation Army, Nicole leads various community support initiatives including drop-in spaces, emergency relief programs, and holistic support services that foster belonging and transformation. She is particularly passionate about breaking down stigmas around homelessness through storytelling and partnership-building, emphasizing that sustainable change comes through both practical assistance and genuine human connection.

Muhammad Patel is a dedicated community leader who has spent the past decade helping people experiencing homelessness in Perth and Fremantle, Australia. Originally from Zambia and guided by his Muslim faith, Patel joined a grassroots food distribution initiative in 2014 that transformed from a casual volunteer commitment into a profound personal mission. Through his work, he has developed meaningful friendships with both volunteers and community members while advocating for a more nuanced understanding of homelessness, challenging common misconceptions with compassion and firsthand experience.

Aaron Stapleton, 42, experienced a dramatic life reversal from managing a company to homelessness following personal losses, relationship breakdown, and incarceration. Now staying at Vinny's shelter and utilizing their laundry services, Aaron is focused on rebuilding his life while maintaining his dignity and independence.

Tom Bowyer is a dedicated community leader who has spent six years organizing community lunches at Christchurch Cathedral in Newcastle, working alongside local schools and organizations to serve those in need. Initially inspired by his mother, the Dean of the cathedral, during the COVID pandemic, Tom has developed a passionate commitment to volunteer work, particularly focusing on providing essential services like meals and fostering meaningful connections within his community. His leadership extends to mentoring young volunteers and advocating for social justice, drawing from his own early experiences of community service with his mother to inspire the next generation of community-minded individuals.

Tig Hall is a dedicated community volunteer and former public servant who has spent eight years serving with Orange Sky, a mobile laundry service for people in need. Working as a disability transport driver for CDC Transport and self-described "queen being clown," Tig brings warmth and humor while fostering meaningful connections with both volunteers and service users. Beyond the practical support of laundry services, Tig has helped create a welcoming atmosphere where people can find friendship, share their stories, and feel part of a caring community.

Michael Young, known as "Bear," is a resilient leader and community advocate whose journey has taken him from seafaring and culinary entrepreneurship to becoming a valued voice within social support networks. After experiencing personal setbacks including a workplace accident and subsequent challenges, Bear found renewed purpose through organizations like Orange Sky and St Vincent's, where he now helps others navigate similar struggles while championing the importance of genuine human connection. Drawing from his father's teachings of independence and his extensive world travels, Bear embodies the balance between preserving traditional values and embracing positive change, demonstrating how authentic care and community support can transform lives.

Amanda Mundell is a tenancy manager at Pacific Link Housing and dedicated community volunteer who transformed her personal experiences with adversity into a platform for helping others. After overcoming significant challenges as a single mother, she completed a housing certification and now assists individuals facing similar circumstances she once encountered. Through her volunteer work with Orange Sky and as a spokesperson for the Good Box, Amanda demonstrates the power of resilience and giving back, while inspiring others with her message that positive change is possible.

Kellie Knight is a dedicated Orange Sky volunteer and government employee based in Rockhampton, where she has lived for over 25 years. As a mother of three, she devotes her free time to helping provide laundry services and meaningful connections to people experiencing homelessness, emphasizing the importance of empathetic listening and non-judgmental support. Kellie is passionate about expanding access to essential services in rural and remote communities, and finds deep fulfillment in connecting with others while helping them maintain dignity through clean laundry and compassionate conversation.

Suzanne Evans is a dedicated volunteer at Christchurch Cathedral's community meal program, where she has served the homeless and underprivileged for over a decade. Drawing from her family background as the granddaughter of priests and her education at the local grammar school, she helps coordinate a volunteer-driven initiative that serves up to 93 people fortnightly, while also mentoring students who participate in the service program. Suzanne's commitment to creating a welcoming space goes beyond providing meals, as she works to foster dignity, social connection, and support for community members in need, including homeless individuals, struggling families, and those seeking rehabilitation.

Brontee Lawson is a passionate social worker and advocate who works at the intersection of justice, disability, and community support in Tasmania. With advanced degrees in social work, psychology, and criminology, she dedicates her professional life to supporting individuals involved in the prison system and community corrections, while also volunteering with Orange Sky to assist people experiencing homelessness. Through both her career and volunteer work, Brontee focuses on building meaningful connections and recognizing the inherent dignity, resilience, and potential in every person she serves, particularly those facing cognitive challenges or systemic barriers.

Kay Peterson is a retired educator and librarian from Hobart, Tasmania who brings her passion for connecting with people to her volunteer work with Orange Sky. Drawing from her background in teaching and library services, she dedicates her time to providing essential laundry services while fostering meaningful conversations with community members. Kay's commitment to giving back and building relationships exemplifies her belief in the transformative power of clean clothes and genuine human connection.

Paul Kayne is a retired electronics technician and dedicated community volunteer based in Hobart, Tasmania. After moving to Hobart eight years ago, he found purpose in giving back through Orange Sky's mobile laundry service, where he helps provide clean clothes to people experiencing disadvantage while fostering meaningful connections through conversation. An avid bushwalker who believes in the power of supporting others after having "a lucky life," Paul brings technical expertise and genuine compassion to his volunteer work, recognizing how clean clothes can make a significant difference in people's lives and wellbeing.

Celeste Gibbs is a dedicated public servant working in diplomacy and treaty implementation between Australia and Timor-Leste, while also pursuing her master's degree in international relations. As a long-term volunteer with Orange Sky and weekend radio station host, she brings a deep commitment to building community connections and preserving human dignity, particularly through her work supporting people experiencing homelessness. Her multifaceted approach to service, whether through diplomatic channels or grassroots volunteering, reflects her passionate belief in the power of diverse stories and meaningful human connection to create positive change.

Shaun Thomas Rogers is a dedicated community services professional who transitioned from radio broadcasting to focus on making a direct impact in people's lives. Drawing from his extensive volunteering experience, he now works to provide essential support services including food assistance, crisis intervention, and practical aid to community members in need. Through his role, Rogers emphasizes the importance of both practical support and meaningful human connection, helping create a welcoming space where people can access vital resources while feeling heard and valued.

Kylie is a community-minded volunteer from the Western Sydney Mountains area who dedicates her time to supporting local organizations and helping others in need. Despite facing her own challenges, she actively contributes to neighborhood centers and laundry services, while advocating for better resources and understanding for those experiencing homelessness. Drawing from personal experience, Kylie offers valuable insights into community support systems and emphasizes the importance of accessible services, temporary housing solutions, and mental health resources in creating positive change.
Tracy McCartney is a dedicated Orange Sky volunteer in Adelaide, bringing warmth and connection to the community through laundry services and genuine conversation.

Ana King is a dedicated Health Programs Coordinator at Bega Aboriginal Health Service, where she has served the Goldfields community for over 16 years in various roles. Drawing from her extensive experience starting in the Crèche and expanding into broader community health initiatives, she coordinates vital programs including Connected Beginnings, Community Safety and Wellbeing, and Orange Sky services. Ana's passionate commitment to education, community connection, and collaborative service delivery has helped strengthen support systems for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families throughout the region, while her emphasis on dignity and compassion continues to create positive change for vulnerable community members.

Marcus Barlow is a thoughtful community member and former security guard who brings deep insight to conversations about social support and mental health. Drawing from his Christian background and personal experiences with PTSD, he has become a longtime participant and advocate of Orange Sky's services, where he values both the practical assistance and meaningful connections formed through genuine conversation. Marcus exemplifies resilience through his structured approach to wellbeing, maintaining an active lifestyle through reading, exercise, and regular community engagement while offering wisdom about the importance of proactive compassion in society.

Kelly Benjamin is a dedicated Orange Sky volunteer in Perth, Australia, who has been serving her community since 2019 after being inspired by the organization's founders at a Flight Centre conference. Drawing from her own experience immigrating from South Africa at age 17 and appreciating the opportunities found in Australia, she channels her gratitude into meaningful service at the Moore Street shift, where she helps create connections and provide support to friends experiencing homelessness. Kelly's commitment to friendship, empathy, and "making the unseen feel seen" exemplifies the transformative power of volunteering and community building.

Colin Banks is a resilient individual who has navigated life's challenges while living in various communities across Australia, from Sydney to Harvey Bay. Despite experiencing homelessness, he maintains his independence through life in his well-equipped caravan, where he demonstrates remarkable adaptability and practical resourcefulness. Colin values community connection and appreciates services like Orange Sky that provide both practical assistance and meaningful social interaction, while offering thoughtful perspectives on how society can better support those experiencing housing instability.

Greg Cooke is a dedicated Orange Sky volunteer in Hobart, Tasmania, who has been serving his community for nearly a decade since retiring. As part of the Monday shift crew, he finds deep fulfillment in providing laundry services and meaningful conversation to those who visit the van, while particularly valuing the strong bonds formed with his fellow volunteers. When not volunteering, Greg pursues his passion for travel across Australia in his VW Combi, having lived in various territories and continuing to explore new places, with a particular fondness for Northern New South Wales and Cairns.

Graham Williams is a dedicated volunteer leader with Orange Sky, where he has spent over four years providing laundry services and fostering meaningful connections with people experiencing hardship. After retiring from his career, he found renewed purpose through his Monday morning shifts, where his approach of combining reliability, compassion, and humor helps create a welcoming environment for those in transition. Graham's leadership style emphasizes the importance of preserving human dignity while building genuine relationships, demonstrating how small acts of service can strengthen community bonds and support those navigating challenging circumstances.

Tracy McIntyre is a dedicated volunteer with Orange Sky, bringing warmth and understanding to her role supporting people experiencing homelessness and hardship in Adelaide. Drawing from her background in education and community work, she contributes her time and compassion through regular shifts operating mobile laundry services, while fostering meaningful connections with both friends of the service and fellow volunteers. Tracy's commitment to positively impacting her community is reflected in her thoughtful approach to service and her appreciation for the dignity-preserving work of Orange Sky.

Dena Rundle serves as the Social Support Manager at Bega, where she has dedicated 14 years to improving community wellbeing, rising from her initial role as a cleaner through determination and leadership. As a born-and-bred local with Torres Strait Islander and domestic worker heritage, she brings deep cultural understanding to her work, focusing on education, family support, and bridging gaps in Indigenous services through innovative community engagement programs. Dena's visionary leadership style emphasizes hands-on community connection through yarning sessions and practical support initiatives, while her commitment to preserving cultural traditions while embracing progress has made a lasting impact on social wellbeing and community cohesion in the region.

Edward Campion is a resilient individual who has navigated housing insecurity while maintaining strong connections to his community support networks. Through his experiences with organizations like Orange Sky, St. Benedict's Community Center, and various social services, he demonstrates the importance of both practical assistance and meaningful human connection in creating positive change. Recently transitioning into his own housing, Edward offers valuable insights about the role of community services and social support in fostering mental wellbeing and personal progress.

Chris is a New Zealand-born builder and community advocate who immigrated to Australia in 1981, where he established himself in the construction industry along Queensland's coast. Drawing from his extensive experience in high-rise construction and his journey from Nelson to various Australian communities, he now focuses on social advocacy and community engagement, particularly around youth programs and local government initiatives. Despite facing health challenges, Chris maintains an active voice in his community while strengthening family bonds and sharing his unique perspective on Australian-New Zealand relations and social issues.

Steve Sutton is a retired finance professional who transitioned from a 36-year corporate career to becoming a dedicated volunteer with Orange Sky, a mobile laundry service for people experiencing homelessness. Drawing from his business background, he serves as a van leader and actively contributes to the organization's mission while gaining deeper insights into housing affordability challenges and community needs. Through his volunteer work across multiple locations, Steve has developed a profound understanding of homelessness issues and finds fulfillment in fostering meaningful connections with both friends of the service and fellow volunteers.

Emily Bell is a dedicated team leader and volunteer with Orange Sky in Bundaberg, Queensland, where she helps provide free laundry services and meaningful conversation to community members in need. Drawing from her experience as a mother and her background in community service, Emily brings thoughtful leadership and organizational skills to her role while advocating for greater support for vulnerable populations. She is particularly passionate about building connections with service users and working to expand Orange Sky's reach to help more people experiencing hardship in the Bundaberg region.

Freddy Wai is a resilient refugee from Papua New Guinea who received asylum in Australia in 2024, bringing with him deep insights about human rights, community connection, and personal growth. Despite facing significant challenges including homelessness and cultural adjustment, he maintains an optimistic perspective and deep appreciation for Australia's beauty and the support services available to those in need. Freddy's story exemplifies courage and perseverance as he works to build a new life while holding onto his cultural heritage, and he aspires to give back to his community through volunteer work once he feels more established.

Georgie Ibbott is a dedicated Orange Sky volunteer in Tasmania, where she helps provide laundry services to hospital patients and supports community members in need. As a born-and-bred Tasmanian who has worked and studied in the region her entire life, she brings a deep understanding of local needs to her volunteer work, particularly valuing the meaningful connections she forms with service users and fellow volunteers. Through her decade of service at multiple locations including North Hobart and local hospitals, Georgie demonstrates her commitment to making essential services accessible while advocating for volunteer engagement and sustainable community support.

Greg Graham is a retired professional from the heavy earth moving and mining equipment sector who has dedicated his post-career life to community service through Orange Sky, an organization providing mobile laundry services to those in need. Drawing from his North Queensland roots and extensive industry experience, Greg has spent over two years building meaningful connections with community members in Newcastle, offering both practical assistance and compassionate support. His commitment to breaking down social barriers and fostering understanding between different community segments reflects his belief in the power of face-to-face interaction and personal engagement to create positive change.

Jared Keating is a dedicated driver volunteer with Orange Sky in Adelaide, bringing compassion and understanding to his role serving communities in need. A former educator who transitioned to volunteering after retiring in 2021, Jared demonstrates a deep appreciation for the power of human connection and the importance of treating everyone with dignity, particularly noting how many people are "just two disasters away" from needing support services. His experience in schools and commitment to community service has helped him foster meaningful relationships with both fellow volunteers and friends of the service, while advocating for greater awareness of social inequity.

Jiri Pasovsky is a retired mining engineer and former taxi driver who immigrated to Australia in 1970, learning English and building a successful career despite starting with just a few words of the language. After graduating from the Calgary School of Mines with dual disciplines in 1978, he went on to manage one of Australia's largest gold mining plants before transitioning into real estate and later spending three decades as a taxi driver. Now 80 years old, Pasovsky remains resilient and forward-looking, drawing on his diverse life experiences to give back to his community through volunteer work.

Nichole Ann Dobson is a community leader and advocate who has dedicated herself to serving vulnerable populations through programs like Orange Sky and her church's Second Bite initiative. Drawing from her experiences raising four children in Brunswick Heads and navigating housing challenges in New South Wales, she brings deep empathy and wisdom to her volunteer work. Nichole champions the power of kindness and human connection, emphasizing how volunteer-led services can create meaningful impact while preserving core values of compassion and dignity for all community members.

Nici Toll is a dedicated youth worker and community advocate in Gladstone who channels her passion for helping others through her work with PCYC and local outreach programs. Drawing from her own experiences and journey through mental health challenges, she has built meaningful connections with vulnerable youth and community members through free barbecues, drop-in centers, and conversation spaces. Nici's strength lies in her ability to listen without judgment and create welcoming environments where people feel heard, combining her professional role with volunteer work to foster positive change in her community.

Bec Smyth is a retired teacher and dedicated Orange Sky volunteer based in Adelaide, bringing a wealth of diverse experience from living across Australia, England, and Hong Kong. Through her volunteer work, she has developed meaningful connections with community members while helping provide essential laundry services and companionship, approaching her role with warmth, empathy and a deep appreciation for the dignity of all people. Her commitment to giving time rather than material things has fostered lasting friendships with both volunteers and service users, demonstrating the profound impact that simple acts of kindness can have on building community.

Kevin Vos is a community leader and chaplain serving in Western Australia's goldfields region, where he works alongside his wife Veronica to provide spiritual and practical support to those experiencing hardship. Drawing from his own experiences of overcoming adversity, Kevin helps operate a community hub that offers essential services like laundry facilities, showers, and meals while fostering an environment of unconditional acceptance and dignity. His work emphasizes the power of human connection and basic kindness, demonstrating how simple acts of compassion can transform lives and build stronger communities.

Paul Gordan is a seasoned leader at Horizon with over a decade of experience managing maintenance contracts across multiple Australian locations including Brisbane, Toowoomba, and Mackay.
